To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the intergalactic gas is enriched to 0.1 - 0.3 solar, that a substantial fraction of the dust is removed from galaxies and that it may be responsible for a significant fraction of the cosmic infrared background.

the dust-to-metal ratio in intergalactic space could be significantly lower than that in galaxies; that the reddening by this dust is too gray to have yet been detected by its effects on Type Ia supernovae; that the reddened supernovae at 0.5 < z < 1 could be dimmed enough by intergalactic dust to explain the observed dimming without the need for cosmic acceleration; that the reddenering is not detectable by the reddening of galaxies

(1) the observed dimming of type Ia supernovae at redshifts z 0.4 is most likely due to dust reddening and/or extinction in the intergalactic space; and (2) the dust-to-metal ratio f is 0.3 0.7, and the minimum grain radius is 0.1 0.5 μm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin and evolution of galaxies and their intergalactic environment in a cosmological context.
the origin and properties of intergalactic dust and its effects on the cosmic star formation history, the evolution of the universe and the CIB.
the evolution of dust in the universe, and its impact on cosmology, galaxy counts and the CIB.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the IGM is not dusty enough to explain the dimming of Type Ia supernovae at 0.3 < z < 0.8, but it is dusty enough to be cosmically significant, and the dust may be detectable by observations of supernovae and of the CIB.
the intergalactic gas has a significant metal content, and that the intergalactically ejected dust is likely to be important in the evolution of the universe.
the intergalactic cosmic dust is either not there at all, or it is there in a form which is not yet understood, or it is not yet detectable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IGM is likely to contain a substantial amount of dust, which could have important effects on observations of high redshift supernovae and galaxy counts.
intergalactic dust is a viable alternative to cosmic acceleration, but it is not yet established.
the observed Type Ia SNe dimming at z 0 5 can be explained by intergalactic dust without invoking dark energy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dust-to-metal ratio in the IGM is probably much lower than in galaxies and may be as low as 1/4.
the dust-to-metal ratio in the IGM is probably much smaller than in galaxies, implying that dust is destroyed during ejection from galaxies or in the intergalactic gas.
dust can play an important role in Type Ia supernovae observations and in the CIB.
